newsitem.title: UK: Records of 19th century English elopement on sale.
newsitem.headline: Records of 19th century English elopement on sale.

text.p: Intimate details of secretive, forbidden and even scandalous marriages performed in the 19th Century Scottish equivalent of Las Vegas will be sold at auction on Thursday.

Gretna Green on the Scottish borders became popular as the elopement capital of Britain in the early 1800's for English couples seeking a quick wedding with no questions asked and without any frills or parental consent.

"This is the first time records such as these have been auctioned on the open market. They are the earliest records of marriages from Gretna Green in existence," said Andrew McCoull of auctioneers Anderson and Garland.

After a 1754 bill outlawed unlicensed marriage in England, couples fled to the village in horse-drawn carriages for quickie weddings which under Scottish law only required that they declare their wish to marry before witnesses.
Among the most scandalous unions was the 1818 wedding of former lord chancellor Thomas Erskine who married his housekeeper, the mother of his illegitimate child.

Erskine's sons from his first marriage, which lasted 35 years, tried to have their father committed to an asylum before he disguised himself as a woman and fled with his lover to Gretna Green where he was married by Parson David Lang.
Lang, his son Simon and later his grandson William all became famous for their marriage ceremonies.
One Lang marriage resulted in a sensational trial after bridegroom Edward Gibbon-Wakefield abducted a wealthy 15-year-old heiress from her boarding school in 1826 before marrying her in Gretna Green.
He and his accomplice were sentenced to three years in jail.
"The Langs were three of several "priests' who competed to marry hundreds of couples who fled across the borders," McCoull said in a statement.
Like all the parsons, the Langs, whose records are being auctioned, arranged everything from witnesses to receptions and even inns for the wedding night.

Bidding on the documents is expected to start at 2,000 pounds ($3,314) but McCoull said the sales has attracted interest from as far away as the United States. He expects the four ledgers and loose papers of marriages from 1794 to 1874 to reach "tens of thousands of pounds (dollars)".
